concepts.name: BERT
concepts.summary: A language representation model pre-trained on unlabeled text so that every layer conditions on both left and right context, then fine-tuned with one extra output layer per task.
concepts.explanation: The paper introduces BERT as a two-stage recipe: pre-train a deep [[transformer-encoder]] on [[unlabeled-text]] with a [[masked-language-model]] and a [[next-sentence-prediction]] objective, then fine-tune all parameters on a labeled task with a single output layer on top. The authors claim this removes the need for heavily engineered task-specific architectures, and report new best results on eleven NLP tasks. They describe BERT as conceptually simple; the argument rests on ablations rather than on machinery that is new in itself. Code and pre-trained models are released.

concepts.name: Transfer learning
concepts.summary: Training a model on one large task or corpus and reusing its parameters on a different, usually smaller, target task.
concepts.explanation: The paper treats transfer as the organising idea behind the work it reviews: a model trained once on plentiful data supplies representations that a target task has too little labeled data to learn alone. Section 2 splits the sources into [[unlabeled-text]] and labeled data from large supervised tasks. The conclusion states that recent gains from language model transfer make unsupervised pre-training an integral part of many language understanding systems, and frames the paper's contribution as generalising those findings from deep unidirectional to deep bidirectional architectures.

concepts.name: Language model pre-training
concepts.summary: Training a model on a language modeling objective over unlabeled text, then reusing it for downstream NLP tasks.
concepts.explanation: The introduction states that language model pre-training has improved many NLP tasks, citing work from Dai and Le (2015) through ELMo, [[openai-gpt]] and ULMFiT. Because the objective needs no labels, the corpus can be far larger than any annotated dataset. The paper notes that before BERT both families of transfer methods shared the same pre-training objective — a unidirectional language model — and that shared choice is what it argues is the limiting factor.

concepts.name: Unlabeled text
concepts.summary: Plain running text with no human annotation, used as the training signal for objectives that predict text from text.
concepts.explanation: Left-to-right language modeling, masked language modeling and [[next-sentence-prediction]] all construct their own targets from the text, so no labeling effort is needed. That is what allows pre-training corpora measured in billions of words while labeled task datasets stay in the thousands or hundreds of thousands. The paper uses "unsupervised" in the same sense in its section titles.

concepts.name: Downstream task
concepts.summary: The labeled end task a pre-trained representation is applied to, such as question answering, entailment or tagging.
concepts.explanation: The paper divides downstream tasks into sentence-level ones, which predict a relationship over whole inputs, and token-level ones, which need fine-grained output per token. That split matters to the argument: unidirectional pre-training is called sub-optimal for the first and potentially very harmful for the second. BERT's design goal is that the same pre-trained body serve all of them with only inputs and outputs changed.

concepts.name: Sentence-level tasks
concepts.summary: Tasks producing one label for the whole input, such as inference, paraphrase detection and sentiment classification.
concepts.explanation: The output is a single decision about the input rather than per-token structure, so the model needs a representation that summarises the sentence or pair. In BERT these are handled by reading the final [CLS] vector into an output layer. The paper notes GPT's left-to-right restriction is sub-optimal here, since a summary position can only see text to its left.

concepts.name: Token-level tasks
concepts.summary: Tasks where the model must produce output at each token, such as named entity recognition and extractive question answering.
concepts.explanation: The model emits a decision per token rather than per input, so the individual final hidden vectors are what get read. The paper argues unidirectional pre-training could be very harmful here, because deciding about a token often needs context from both sides. Extractive QA is the running example: span boundaries depend on words after them as much as before.

concepts.name: Natural language inference
concepts.summary: Given a premise and a hypothesis, decide whether the hypothesis is entailed by, contradicts, or is neutral with respect to the premise.
concepts.explanation: The paper cites SNLI and MultiNLI as the datasets that made this a standard sentence-pair benchmark, and it appears twice in the argument: as a task BERT is evaluated on, and in Section 2.3 as a source of supervised transfer. MNLI uses three labels; RTE and WNLI are binary variants. As a pair task it maps directly onto BERT's packed two-segment input.

concepts.name: Question answering
concepts.summary: Given a question and a passage, produce the answer; in the extractive form used here, mark the passage span that answers it.
concepts.explanation: The paper treats QA as the sharpest case for bidirectionality: predicting where a span starts and ends needs context from both directions, so a left-to-right model is handicapped. It is listed in the abstract as a task family BERT is fine-tuned for, and SQuAD supplies the headline numbers.

concepts.name: Named entity recognition
concepts.summary: Labeling each token with whether it belongs to a name of a person, organisation, location and so on, and which type.
concepts.explanation: The paper uses NER as its example of a task needing per-token output, and as the testbed for the feature-based ablation. Because the output is one label per token, the model must read every token's final hidden vector, and a rule is needed for mapping sub-word pieces back to words.

concepts.name: CoNLL-2003 NER
concepts.summary: The shared-task dataset used as the standard NER benchmark, and the testbed for BERT's feature-based and masking ablations.
concepts.explanation: Its label set and evaluation conventions are what make NER numbers comparable across papers. BERT uses a case-preserving WordPiece model here, since capitalisation is a strong entity cue, and feeds in the maximal document context the data provides rather than just the sentence being tagged. Both are stated as setup, not tested as variables. The paper reports BERT_LARGE performing competitively with state-of-the-art methods.

concepts.name: Tagging without a CRF layer
concepts.summary: NER is formulated as tagging, but the output layer is a plain per-token classifier with no conditional random field on top.
concepts.explanation: A CRF is standard practice for sequence tagging because it models dependencies between adjacent labels and rules out illegal tag sequences. The paper says it follows standard practice in formulating NER as tagging but deliberately omits the CRF, so each token's label is predicted independently. That keeps the task-specific machinery minimal, which is the point the experiments section is making.

concepts.name: First sub-token as the token representation
concepts.summary: When WordPiece splits a word, the first piece's final hidden vector is what the tag classifier reads.
concepts.explanation: NER labels are defined over words but BERT's outputs are per sub-token, so a mapping rule is needed. The paper takes the first sub-token's vector and drops the rest. This is a convention, not a result; no alternative pooling is compared.

concepts.name: Feature-based vs. fine-tuning transfer
concepts.summary: The paper's taxonomy of the two ways pre-trained representations were applied downstream: as extra input features, or by fine-tuning the whole model.
concepts.explanation: The introduction sets up the two strategies as the map of prior work, with ELMo as the feature-based example and [[openai-gpt]] as the fine-tuning example. The paper stresses that both share the same pre-training objective — a unidirectional language model — so the difference is in how the weights are used downstream, not in what is learned. BERT is positioned as an improvement to the fine-tuning branch, and Appendix A.4 restates the split when comparing the three models.

concepts.name: Feature-based approach
concepts.summary: Keep the pre-trained model fixed and feed its representations into a separate task-specific architecture as extra input features.
concepts.explanation: ELMo is the paper's example. The pre-trained weights are not updated; the task model, which may be large and hand-designed, consumes the pre-trained vectors alongside its own embeddings. Each new task therefore still needs its own architecture, which the paper counts as a cost. Section 5.3 tests BERT used this way.

concepts.name: Task-specific architecture
concepts.summary: A model designed by hand for one task, into which pre-trained representations are inserted as features.
concepts.explanation: The paper's second stated contribution is that pre-trained representations reduce the need for many heavily engineered task-specific architectures. It claims BERT is the first fine-tuning based representation model to reach state of the art on a large suite of both sentence-level and [[token-level-tasks|token-level tasks]] while outperforming such architectures. The claim is about breadth: one configuration covering tasks that previously each had their own design.

concepts.name: Fine-tuning approach
concepts.summary: Add minimal task-specific parameters on top of the pre-trained model and train all pre-trained parameters further on labeled task data.
concepts.explanation: [[openai-gpt]] is the paper's example, with Dai and Le (2015) and Howard and Ruder (2018) as earlier instances. Section 2.2 states the advantage plainly: few parameters need to be learned from scratch. The paper argues the unidirectionality limitation bites hardest here, because the same restricted architecture has to serve both as a language model during pre-training and as the task model afterwards.

concepts.name: Minimal task-specific parameters
concepts.summary: The design goal that adapting to a new task should add as few new weights as possible.
concepts.explanation: The abstract's version is that the pre-trained model can be fine-tuned with just [[task-specific-output-layer|one additional output layer]], without substantial [[task-specific-architecture|task-specific architecture]] modifications. Fewer new parameters means less to estimate from limited labeled data and one code path across tasks. It also makes cross-task comparison cleaner, since what differs is mostly the data.

concepts.name: ELMo
concepts.summary: A feature-based model that extracts context-sensitive word features from separately trained left-to-right and right-to-left language models, concatenating the two directions.
concepts.explanation: Section 2.1 describes ELMo as generalising word embedding research along a different dimension: instead of one vector per word type, each token gets a representation depending on its sentence. Plugged into existing task architectures, it advanced the state of the art on benchmarks including [[question-answering]], sentiment analysis and NER. The paper's criticism is not that ELMo is unidirectional but that its bidirectionality is shallow, since neither direction is ever computed with the other's context available.

concepts.name: OpenAI GPT
concepts.summary: A fine-tuning approach that pre-trains a left-to-right Transformer language model on unlabeled text, then fine-tunes it on downstream tasks; the paper's main comparison point.
concepts.explanation: The paper calls GPT the most comparable existing method and says many of BERT's design decisions were made deliberately to keep the two close. GPT's self-attention is masked so each token attends only to its left, and it is pre-trained as a standard language model. It supplies the size target for BERT_BASE, the contrast case for bidirectionality, and the precedent for using gelu instead of relu. Appendix A.4 lists the remaining differences in corpus, special tokens, batch size and fine-tuning learning rate.

citedFrom.refText: Alec Radford, Karthik Narasimhan, Tim Salimans, and Ilya Sutskever. 2018. Improving language understanding with unsupervised learning. Technical report, OpenAI.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: GPT is the controlled baseline for the whole paper; its architecture, corpus, batch size, learning rate and fine-tuning procedure are what the comparisons are made against.

concepts.name: Contextual representations
concepts.summary: Token vectors that depend on the surrounding sentence, so the same word form gets different vectors in different sentences.
concepts.explanation: Section 2.1 contrasts these with ordinary [[pre-trained-word-embeddings|pre-trained word embeddings]], which assign one vector per word type regardless of use. Section 2.2 describes the fine-tuning branch as pre-training encoders that produce contextual token representations. The interesting question then becomes how much context each representation may see, which is where the paper's unidirectionality argument bites.

concepts.name: context2vec
concepts.summary: A model that learns contextual representations by predicting a single word from both its left and right context using LSTMs.
concepts.explanation: Section 2.1 mentions it as an earlier attempt at using both directions to predict a word, close in spirit to masked language modeling. The paper notes that, like ELMo, it is feature-based and not deeply bidirectional, so it does not remove the constraint BERT targets. It is also one of the two prior results cited on whether bigger pre-trained models help downstream.

concepts.name: Pre-trained word embeddings
concepts.summary: Word vectors learned once from a large unlabeled corpus and reused across tasks, rather than learned per task.
concepts.explanation: Section 2.1 calls them an integral part of modern NLP systems and cites Turian et al. (2010) for the finding that they improve significantly over embeddings learned from scratch. Learning reusable word representations is described as an active area for decades, spanning non-neural methods (Brown et al., 1992) and neural ones (Mikolov et al., 2013; Pennington et al., 2014). They assign one vector per word type, which is the limitation [[contextual-representations]] remove.

concepts.name: Word embeddings
concepts.summary: Dense vectors representing words, learned so that distributional similarity shows up as vector similarity.
concepts.explanation: Assumed background here; it matters only as the thing pre-training first transferred and that [[contextual-representations]] later replaced.

concepts.name: Sentence embeddings
concepts.summary: Fixed-size vectors representing whole sentences, pre-trained from unlabeled text the way word vectors are.
concepts.explanation: Section 2.1 lists three families of objective used to train them: ranking candidate next sentences (Jernite et al., 2017; Logeswaran and Lee, 2018), generating the next sentence's words left to right from a representation of the previous one (Kiros et al., 2015), and denoising-autoencoder derived objectives. The first two are the direct ancestors of BERT's [[next-sentence-prediction]], which also asks a model to relate one span to the following one.

concepts.name: Transfer from supervised data
concepts.summary: Using a model trained on a large labeled task as the starting point for other tasks, as an alternative to pre-training on unlabeled text.
concepts.explanation: Section 2.3 names [[natural-language-inference]] (Conneau et al., 2017) and machine translation (McCann et al., 2017) as effective sources, and points to computer vision, where fine-tuning models pre-trained on ImageNet is described as an effective recipe. The section is short and marks the path the paper is not taking: BERT's transfer comes from [[unlabeled-text]], though the fine-tuning mechanics are the same.

concepts.name: Low-resource tasks
concepts.summary: Tasks with too little labeled data to train a deep model from scratch.
concepts.explanation: The conclusion states that pre-training results enable even low-resource tasks to benefit from deep architectures, because the labeled data only has to adjust an already-trained model rather than fit one from random initialisation. Section 5.2 makes the empirical version of this claim for model size on small datasets.

concepts.name: The unidirectionality constraint
concepts.summary: The paper's central criticism of prior pre-training: standard language models condition on one direction only, which restricts which architectures can be pre-trained and how well they transfer.
concepts.explanation: The argument runs in two steps. First, a standard language model predicts each token from those before it, so the architecture must keep future tokens hidden — in GPT every token attends only to previous tokens. Second, the paper claims this is sub-optimal for [[sentence-level-tasks|sentence-level tasks]] and could be very harmful for token-level ones like [[question-answering]]. It says the limitation bites hardest for fine-tuning approaches, since there the restricted architecture is what gets used downstream.

concepts.name: Left-to-right language model
concepts.summary: A model that assigns probability to text by predicting each token from the tokens that precede it.
concepts.explanation: This is the standard objective and, before BERT, the shared pre-training objective of both transfer branches. Its factorisation forces one-directional information flow: the model must not see the token it is about to predict, or anything after it. The paper notes one advantage it keeps over [[masked-language-model|MLM]] — it makes a prediction at every position, not at 15% of them.

concepts.name: Right-to-left language model
concepts.summary: The mirror image: predict each token from the tokens that follow it.
concepts.explanation: Used in ELMo-style setups as the second half of a bidirectional pair. Section 5.1's objection to that setup for [[question-answering]] turns on direction of information flow: reading a passage right to left, a passage token cannot condition on a question placed before it in the sequence.

concepts.name: Shallow concatenation of two directional models
concepts.summary: Getting both directions by training a left-to-right and a right-to-left model independently and joining their outputs, rather than conditioning on both sides inside the model.
concepts.explanation: The introduction contrasts BERT with ELMo on exactly this point. Because the two models are trained separately, no internal layer ever combines evidence from both sides; the combination happens only at the top. Section 3.1 states it as an intuition rather than a proof that a deep bidirectional model should be strictly more expressive than this, with the empirical case deferred to the ablations.

concepts.name: Why not concatenate LTR and RTL models
concepts.summary: Section 5.1's three stated reasons for not training separate directional models and concatenating them.
concepts.explanation: The reasons given are that it is twice as expensive as a single bidirectional model; that it is non-intuitive for tasks like QA, since a right-to-left model could not condition the answer on the question; and that it is strictly less expressive than a deep bidirectional model, which can use both contexts at every layer. This is an argument the paper makes, not an experiment it runs — no such model appears in Table 5.

concepts.name: Deep bidirectional representations
concepts.summary: Representations in which every layer conditions jointly on both left and right context, rather than combining two one-directional models at the end.
concepts.explanation: The abstract states the goal directly: pre-train deep bidirectional representations by jointly conditioning on both contexts in all layers. "Deep" means the joint conditioning happens at every layer, which is what separates it from ELMo's concatenation and GPT's left-to-right stack. The [[masked-language-model]] is what makes it trainable without a token leaking its own identity. The conclusion frames generalising earlier findings from deep unidirectional to deep bidirectional architectures as the paper's major contribution.

concepts.name: BERT vs. ELMo vs. OpenAI GPT
concepts.summary: Appendix A.4's point-by-point comparison of the three models, covering architecture, transfer strategy, and the training differences that are not architectural.
concepts.explanation: BERT and GPT are fine-tuning approaches while ELMo is feature-based. GPT is named as the most comparable method, and the appendix lists four remaining differences: BERT adds Wikipedia (2,500M words) to GPT's BooksCorpus (800M); BERT learns [CLS], [SEP] and the A/B embeddings during pre-training while GPT introduces its separator only at fine-tuning; batches are 128,000 words against GPT's 32,000 at the same 1M steps; and BERT picks a fine-tuning learning rate per task on dev where GPT used 5e-5 everywhere. Each favours BERT. The paper's answer is that Section 5.1's ablations show most of the gain comes from the pre-training tasks; the four differences are acknowledged rather than controlled away.

concepts.name: BERT's model architecture
concepts.summary: A multi-layer bidirectional Transformer encoder, described by the paper as almost identical to the original Transformer implementation.
concepts.explanation: The paper does not introduce a new architecture: BERT is a stack of [[transformer-encoder]] layers as in Vaswani et al. (2017), released in tensor2tensor, and the authors omit an exhaustive description on the grounds that Transformers have become common. What they specify is size — layers $L$, [[hidden-size-h|hidden size]] $H$, heads $A$ — at two scales. The one architectural point they call out is that self-attention here is bidirectional rather than restricted to left context.

concepts.name: Transformer encoder
concepts.summary: A stack of identical blocks, each combining multi-head self-attention over the whole sequence with a position-wise feed-forward network, mapping token embeddings to contextual vectors.
concepts.explanation: Every layer lets each position attend to every other and mix their representations, then applies the same feed-forward network at each position; layers stack so representations get progressively more contextual. The output is one vector per input token. BERT uses this stack unchanged and points readers to the original paper and to "The Annotated Transformer" rather than re-deriving attention, residual connections or layer normalization.

citedFrom.refText: Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion Jones, Aidan N Gomez, Lukasz Kaiser, and Illia Polosukhin. 2017. Attention is all you need. In NIPS, pages 6000-6010.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: BERT's encoder is this architecture with no described modification; the layer structure, attention and positional encoding are defined there and assumed here.

concepts.name: Self-attention
concepts.summary: The operation by which each position forms its next representation as a weighted combination of all positions it is allowed to attend to.
concepts.explanation: The set of positions a token may attend to is a choice, which is why the same architecture can run one-directionally or bidirectionally. That choice is the technical hinge of the paper's argument: GPT masks attention to previous tokens, BERT does not.

concepts.name: Attention is quadratic in sequence length
concepts.summary: Each layer scores every pair of positions, so doubling the sequence length roughly quadruples attention cost.
concepts.explanation: This is why the paper calls longer sequences disproportionately expensive and trains mostly at 128 tokens before switching to 512. It is a property of the Transformer, not something BERT changes.

concepts.name: Bidirectional self-attention
concepts.summary: Self-attention in which every token may attend to every other token, left and right, at every layer.
concepts.explanation: No attention mask restricts which positions a token can see, so each representation at every layer is built from the entire sequence. The paper marks this as the critical difference from the GPT Transformer. It is also what makes a left-to-right objective unusable and forces the [[masked-language-model|Masked LM]] instead. A footnote notes the convention that the bidirectional version is called an encoder and the left-context-only version a decoder, since the latter can be used for generation.

concepts.name: Constrained (left-context-only) self-attention
concepts.summary: Self-attention masked so each token attends only to tokens on its left, as in the GPT Transformer.
concepts.explanation: With this mask a token's representation never depends on anything after it, which is exactly what a [[left-to-right-language-model|left-to-right language model]] needs to avoid leakage. The paper contrasts it with BERT's unconstrained attention when explaining why BERT_BASE and GPT can be the same size yet behave differently. The constraint is a property of the mask, not of the parameter count.

concepts.name: Model size notation: L, H, A
concepts.summary: The paper's shorthand for a configuration: $L$ layers, hidden size $H$, and $A$ self-attention heads.
concepts.explanation: $L$ is the number of stacked Transformer blocks, $H$ the width of the vectors flowing between them, $A$ the number of attention heads per block. The same notation carries into the ablation tables, so it reads as a compact spec rather than prose. Section 5.2 anchors it against prior work: the largest Transformer in Vaswani et al. (2017) is $L=6, H=1024, A=16$ with 100M encoder parameters, and the largest the authors found anywhere is $L=64, H=512, A=2$ with 235M (Al-Rfou et al., 2018).

concepts.name: Hidden size (H)
concepts.summary: The dimension of the vectors passed between layers; 768 for BERT_BASE and 1024 for BERT_LARGE.
concepts.explanation: $H$ is the width of every token representation inside the model, so the final hidden vectors satisfy $C \in \mathbb{R}^H$ and $T_i \in \mathbb{R}^H$. It also fixes the size of the input embeddings, since those are summed and fed straight into the first layer.

concepts.name: Feed-forward/filter size of 4H
concepts.summary: The inner width of each block's feed-forward network is four times the hidden size: 3072 when $H=768$, 4096 when $H=1024$.
concepts.explanation: A footnote fixes this ratio for all configurations, so the feed-forward size is never an independent knob. Since the parameter count is dominated by these wide inner layers together with the attention projections, the rule is part of what makes the total parameter figures follow from $L$ and $H$.

concepts.name: BERT_BASE and BERT_LARGE
concepts.summary: The two reported configurations: $L=12, H=768, A=12$ with 110M parameters, and $L=24, H=1024, A=16$ with 340M.
concepts.explanation: BERT_BASE was sized to match [[openai-gpt]] so the two can be compared without a capacity confound; BERT_LARGE is the configuration behind the headline results. Pre-training took four days for each: 4 Cloud TPUs (16 chips) for BASE and 16 Cloud TPUs (64 chips) for LARGE, so the larger model gets four times the hardware.

concepts.name: Deliberate size match with OpenAI GPT
concepts.summary: BERT_BASE was sized to equal OpenAI GPT specifically so the comparison isolates bidirectionality rather than capacity.
concepts.explanation: The paper says the two are nearly identical in architecture apart from the attention masking, so the GLUE gap can be read as evidence for bidirectional attention rather than for size. It is candid that other things still differ — [[pre-training-data|pre-training corpus]], [[input-representation]], fine-tuning details — and it addresses those separately through the Section 5.1 ablation rather than by re-running GPT under BERT's conditions.

concepts.name: BERT's two-stage framework
concepts.summary: Pre-train on unlabeled text with self-supervised tasks, then fine-tune every parameter on a labeled task; the same pre-trained weights initialize a separate model per task.
concepts.explanation: In pre-training the model is trained on unlabeled data over two tasks, producing one set of general parameters; this is where nearly all the compute goes, four days on Cloud TPUs. In fine-tuning that checkpoint initializes the model and all parameters are updated on the task's labeled data. The paper presents this as its organizing idea for Section 3, with a [[question-answering|question-answering]] example as the running illustration.

concepts.name: One fine-tuned model per task
concepts.summary: Fine-tuning produces a distinct model for each downstream task, all branching from the same pre-trained starting point.
concepts.explanation: BERT does not end up as a single multi-task model. What is shared is the initialization: every task starts from identical pre-trained weights. This is what lets one expensive pre-training run be amortized across many cheap task-specific runs.

concepts.name: Unified architecture across tasks
concepts.summary: The paper calls it a distinctive feature that the pre-trained architecture and the final downstream architecture differ minimally.
concepts.explanation: Adapting to a task means swapping inputs and outputs, not redesigning the encoder, so almost every parameter carries over from pre-training rather than being initialized randomly. The claim as stated is architectural, not empirical; the evidence that it works appears in the experiments.

concepts.name: Input/output representation
concepts.summary: A single token-sequence format that can represent either one span of text or a pair of spans, so one architecture covers every task.
concepts.explanation: BERT's input is always one token sequence, whether the task supplies one piece of text or two. The sequence begins with [CLS], separates a packed pair with [SEP], and marks which half each token belongs to with a learned segment embedding. Each token's input vector is the sum of its token, segment and [[position-embeddings]]. This is what lets the same pre-trained model be fine-tuned on classification, entailment, tagging and [[question-answering]] without architectural surgery.

concepts.name: "Sentence" as an arbitrary span
concepts.summary: In this paper a "sentence" means any span of contiguous text, not a linguistic sentence, and a "sequence" is the token sequence actually fed to BERT.
concepts.explanation: The paper redefines both words up front. Appendix A.2 adds that the spans sampled for pre-training are typically much longer than single sentences, though they can also be shorter. This matters when reading [[next-sentence-prediction]], which is about two sampled spans rather than two grammatical sentences. The sequence is the unit the model sees, capped at 512 tokens, and batch sizes are quoted in sequences.

concepts.name: WordPiece embeddings
concepts.summary: A subword vocabulary that splits rare words into smaller known pieces, used here with 30,000 tokens.
concepts.explanation: Rather than one embedding per word, WordPiece builds a fixed vocabulary of subword units so any word can be spelled out and nothing falls out of vocabulary; continuation pieces are marked, as in "flight ##less". Two consequences run through the paper: the [[masked-language-model|Masked LM]] predicts over this vocabulary rather than over words, and masking is applied after tokenization with no special consideration given to partial word pieces, so a word can be partly masked.

citedFrom.refText: Yonghui Wu, Mike Schuster, Zhifeng Chen, Quoc V Le, Mohammad Norouzi, Wolfgang Macherey, Maxim Krikun, Yuan Cao, Qin Gao, Klaus Macherey, et al. 2016. Google's neural machine translation system: Bridging the gap between human and machine translation. arXiv:1609.08144.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The algorithm that builds the subword vocabulary and segments text is defined there; this paper gives only the name and the vocabulary size.

concepts.name: 30,000-token vocabulary
concepts.summary: The size of BERT's WordPiece vocabulary, which also fixes the width of the Masked LM output softmax.
concepts.explanation: All text is represented with these 30,000 subword units, and because masked positions feed a softmax over the vocabulary, this is also the number of classes in that prediction. Keeping it small relative to a word vocabulary is what keeps the output layer and embedding table affordable.

concepts.name: [CLS] token
concepts.summary: A special token placed first in every sequence, whose final hidden state is used as the aggregate representation of the whole input.
concepts.explanation: It is not a word from the text, so it carries no lexical meaning and is free to accumulate whatever the encoder needs at sequence level; because attention is bidirectional it can gather from every token at every layer. It does three jobs in the experiments: it supplies the vector for GLUE classification, the per-choice score for SWAG, and in SQuAD 2.0 it doubles as the position standing for "no answer". During pre-training it feeds the [[next-sentence-prediction]] head.

concepts.name: C, the final [CLS] vector
concepts.summary: The paper's notation for the final hidden vector at the [CLS] position, $C \in \mathbb{R}^H$.
concepts.explanation: $C$ appears wherever a whole-sequence output is needed. It has the same width as any other hidden vector; nothing structural distinguishes it except its position and what it is trained to predict. It is just the $T_i$ at position 0, which is why the SQuAD [[start-and-end-vectors]] can score it as a null span.

concepts.name: [SEP] token
concepts.summary: A special token marking the boundary between two packed spans, and closing the sequence.
concepts.explanation: It is the first of the two ways BERT differentiates the halves of a pair; the second is the segment embedding. Appendix A.1's examples show it after each span, so a packed pair reads [CLS] ... [SEP] ... [SEP]. Appendix A.4 notes BERT learns an embedding for it during pre-training while GPT introduces its separator only at fine-tuning time.

concepts.name: Sentence A / sentence B packing
concepts.summary: Two spans are concatenated into one sequence, the first labeled A and the second B, so a pair of texts is handled by the same single-sequence model.
concepts.explanation: The pair is packed rather than encoded separately, so self-attention can relate the two halves directly from the first layer. The same A/B slots are reused at fine-tuning for paraphrase pairs, hypothesis-premise pairs, question-passage pairs, and, degenerately, single-text tasks.

concepts.name: Segment embeddings
concepts.summary: A learned embedding added to every token indicating whether it belongs to sentence A or sentence B.
concepts.explanation: There are two such vectors and every token in a span receives its span's vector, giving the model a signal that does not depend on counting past the separator. Appendix A.2 states the assignment: the first sampled span gets A, the second gets B. For single-text tasks only the A embedding is in play. Appendix A.4 lists them among the things BERT learns in pre-training and GPT does not have.

concepts.name: Position embeddings
concepts.summary: A learned vector per position, added so the model knows token order.
concepts.explanation: Self-attention is order-agnostic, so position information is injected at the input. These are learned rather than fixed, which is why the last 10% of pre-training uses length-512 sequences: positions beyond 128 would otherwise never receive gradients.

concepts.name: Sum of token, segment and position embeddings
concepts.summary: A token's input vector, written $E$, is the elementwise sum of its token embedding, its segment embedding and its position embedding.
concepts.explanation: All three components have width $H$ and are added, so what enters the first layer is one vector per token encoding what the token is, which span it belongs to, and where it sits. Nothing is concatenated, so the input width stays $H$ and the layer stack needs no change. Figure 2 visualizes the construction.

concepts.name: T_i, the final vector for token i
concepts.summary: The output of the top layer at position $i$, $T_i \in \mathbb{R}^H$, described as that token's contextual representation.
concepts.explanation: Every token gets one, and it depends on the whole sequence because attention is unmasked. During pre-training the $T_i$ at masked positions predict the original tokens; during fine-tuning they feed output layers for [[token-level-tasks|token-level tasks]] — dotted with the [[start-and-end-vectors]] for SQuAD, or read at the first sub-token for NER.

concepts.name: Masked LM (MLM)
concepts.summary: BERT's first pre-training task: mask a random 15% of input tokens and train the model to predict the originals from context on both sides.
concepts.explanation: The stated motivation is that a deep bidirectional model should be more expressive than a left-to-right model or a [[shallow-concatenation]], but standard conditional language models cannot be trained bidirectionally without the target leaking into its own context. Masking sidesteps this: the token being predicted is hidden from the input, so the model may attend to everything on both sides without seeing the answer. The final hidden vectors at masked positions feed an output softmax over the vocabulary, trained with cross-entropy against the original tokens. The paper notes this is often called a [[cloze-task]], and that unlike a denoising autoencoder BERT predicts only the masked words.

concepts.name: The "see itself" problem
concepts.summary: Why a standard language model cannot be trained bidirectionally: with context from both sides, the target token reaches its own prediction through the layer stack.
concepts.explanation: If every position attends to every other, then in a multi-layered network the representation used to predict word $i$ has already absorbed word $i$ itself from a neighbour's representation at some intermediate layer. The paper's phrasing is that bidirectional conditioning would let each word indirectly see itself, making the prediction trivial. Note "indirectly": a single-layer model could be masked to avoid this, but depth reintroduces the leak. Masking the input outright is the fix, because then there is nothing at that position to leak.

concepts.name: Cloze task
concepts.summary: The older name for filling in a deleted word from surrounding context, which the paper notes is what MLM amounts to.
concepts.explanation: Taylor (1953) introduced it as a readability measure, not a training objective. The paper names it as the inspiration for masked language modeling, and Section 2.1 notes that Fedus et al. (2018) used the cloze task to improve robustness of text generation models. The aside places [[masked-language-model|MLM]] as a reuse of an existing idea rather than a new one.

concepts.name: 15% masking rate
concepts.summary: In every experiment, 15% of the WordPiece token positions in each sequence are chosen at random for prediction.
concepts.explanation: The rate is uniform and applied after [[wordpiece-tokenization]], with no special handling of partial word pieces, so one piece of a multi-piece word can be masked while the others stay visible. The rate sets a trade-off: predicting more positions gives more signal per sequence but leaves less intact context. It also means each batch supplies predictions for only 15% of tokens, which the paper links to slower convergence.

concepts.name: [MASK] token
concepts.summary: The special placeholder substituted for a word the model must predict.
concepts.explanation: It occupies the position of the hidden word so the model has an input there but no information about which word it was. It exists only during pre-training: the token never appears during fine-tuning, which is the source of the mismatch the 80/10/10 recipe is meant to soften.

concepts.name: Pre-train / fine-tune mismatch
concepts.summary: Any difference between the conditions a model was pre-trained under and those it meets at fine-tuning; here, [MASK] appears constantly in pre-training and never afterwards.
concepts.explanation: If every chosen position were replaced with [MASK], the model could learn to produce useful representations only when it sees that marker. The 80/10/10 recipe is the mitigation, and the paper says it mitigates rather than removes the problem. The same idea drives another choice: in the LTR ablation the left-only attention constraint had to be kept at fine-tuning time, because removing it introduced a mismatch that degraded results. The mismatch is described as more damaging in the feature-based setting, where the model cannot adjust its representations to compensate.

concepts.name: The 80/10/10 masking recipe
concepts.summary: Of the 15% chosen positions, 80% become [MASK], 10% become a random token, and 10% are left unchanged; the original token is the target in all three cases.
concepts.explanation: Appendix A.1 works the example "my dog is hairy" through all three branches, replacing "hairy" with "apple" in the random case. The argument for the mix is that the encoder does not know which words it will be asked to predict or which have been replaced, so it must keep a distributional contextual representation of every input token rather than trusting unmarked positions. Because random replacement touches only 1.5% of all tokens, the paper says this does not seem to harm language understanding — a hedge, with the comparison deferred to Appendix C.2.

concepts.name: Output softmax over the vocabulary
concepts.summary: Masked positions' final hidden vectors are projected to a distribution over the 30,000 WordPiece tokens and trained with cross-entropy on the original token.
concepts.explanation: This is the same output head shape a language model uses; what differs is which positions are scored and what context they saw. Only the chosen 15% of positions contribute to the loss.

concepts.name: Contrast with denoising autoencoders
concepts.summary: Unlike a denoising autoencoder, BERT predicts only the masked words rather than reconstructing the whole input.
concepts.explanation: A denoising autoencoder corrupts an input and trains the model to reproduce the entire clean version; BERT corrupts the same way but scores only the corrupted positions. The paper draws the line explicitly against Vincent et al. (2008). One consequence is fewer predictions per sequence, which it connects to needing more pre-training steps.

concepts.name: MLM's slower convergence
concepts.summary: Predicting only 15% of tokens per batch gives fewer gradient signals per step, so MLM converges slightly slower than a left-to-right model — but reaches higher accuracy almost immediately.
concepts.explanation: An LTR objective gets a signal from every position, an [[masked-language-model|MLM]] only from masked ones, so per step it extracts less supervision from the same text. Appendix C.1 reports that the MLM model does converge marginally slower but begins to outperform the LTR model on absolute MNLI Dev accuracy almost immediately, so the slower convergence never makes LTR the better choice at any point on the curve shown. The evidence is one curve on one task.

concepts.name: Next Sentence Prediction (NSP)
concepts.summary: BERT's second pre-training task: a binary classification of whether span B actually followed span A in the corpus, predicted from the [CLS] vector.
concepts.explanation: The stated motivation is that tasks like [[question-answering]] and inference depend on the relationship between two sentences, which language modeling does not directly capture. The task can be trivially generated from any monolingual corpus: half the time B is the real next span, half the time a random one. The paper calls it simple, reports the final model reaching 97-98% accuracy on NSP itself against a 50% chance baseline, and points to Section 5.1 rather than that number for evidence that it helps downstream.

concepts.name: IsNext / NotNext labels
concepts.summary: The two NSP labels: B genuinely followed A, or B is a random span from elsewhere in the corpus, balanced 50/50.
concepts.explanation: Appendix A.1 gives worked examples of both, with masking applied on top so the two pre-training tasks share the same input. Because negatives are drawn at random from the corpus rather than from nearby text, many NotNext pairs differ in topic, which makes the task easier than a discourse-coherence test would be.

concepts.name: C is not a sentence representation without fine-tuning
concepts.summary: A footnote cautioning that the pre-trained [CLS] vector should not be read as a general-purpose sentence embedding.
concepts.explanation: The vector has only ever been asked one question — did B follow A — so whatever it encodes is shaped by that question. Using it off the shelf as a sentence embedding is not something the paper supports.

concepts.name: Transferring all parameters, not just sentence embeddings
concepts.summary: The paper's stated difference from prior sentence-representation objectives: those transfer only sentence embeddings downstream, while BERT transfers every parameter.
concepts.explanation: [[next-sentence-prediction|NSP]] is described as closely related to the objectives of Jernite et al. (2017) and Logeswaran and Lee (2018), which rank or discriminate candidate next sentences. The distinction drawn is about what moves downstream. It is the framework's claim applied at the pair level, and it is asserted rather than measured here.

concepts.name: Pre-training procedure
concepts.summary: The concrete recipe: corpus, how input sequences are generated, batch size and step count, optimizer settings, and the sequence-length schedule.
concepts.explanation: Appendix A.2 spells out what Section 3.1 leaves at the level of ideas: sampling and packing two spans, masking after tokenization, 256-sequence batches of up to 512 tokens for 1,000,000 steps, Adam with warmup and linear decay, dropout 0.1 and gelu, the summed loss, the hardware, and the two-phase length schedule. Together these are what a reproduction would need.

concepts.name: Pre-training corpus
concepts.summary: BooksCorpus (800M words) plus English Wikipedia (2,500M words), roughly 3.3 billion words in total.
concepts.explanation: The paper says its procedure largely follows existing literature and names two sources. For Wikipedia only the text passages are kept; lists, tables and headers are ignored, since those carry little sentence-to-sentence continuity. The 3.3 billion figure is what makes 1,000,000 steps at 128,000 tokens per batch roughly 40 epochs.

concepts.name: BooksCorpus (800M words)
concepts.summary: A corpus of unpublished books forming the smaller half of BERT's pre-training data, and the whole of GPT's.
concepts.explanation: Its relevance is structural as much as textual: books are long continuous documents, which is what the document-level requirement calls for. Being the shared half of the two corpora, it is the part of the data that does not distinguish BERT from GPT.

citedFrom.refText: Yukun Zhu, Ryan Kiros, Rich Zemel, Ruslan Salakhutdinov, Raquel Urtasun, Antonio Torralba, and Sanja Fidler. 2015. Aligning books and movies: Towards story-like visual explanations by watching movies and reading books. In ICCV, pages 19-27.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: What the 800M-word corpus contains and how it was assembled bears on the document-level claim and on any attempt to reproduce pre-training.

concepts.name: English Wikipedia (2,500M words)
concepts.summary: The larger half of the pre-training data, with only running text kept.
concepts.explanation: Appendix A.4 lists this as the first of the four differences between BERT's and GPT's training: BERT sees roughly four times as much text, of a different kind. The appendix does not try to separate the effect of the extra data from the effect of the objectives; it points to Section 5.1's ablations instead.

concepts.name: Document-level corpus
concepts.summary: The requirement that pre-training text keep documents intact, so long contiguous sequences can be sampled.
concepts.explanation: The paper calls it critical to use a document-level corpus rather than a shuffled sentence-level one. Two things depend on it: [[masked-language-model|MLM]] benefits from wide context up to 512 tokens, and [[next-sentence-prediction|NSP]] needs real adjacency to construct IsNext examples at all. A corpus of independently shuffled sentences would supply neither.

concepts.name: Billion Word Benchmark (as a counter-example)
concepts.summary: The shuffled sentence-level corpus the paper names as the kind of data it deliberately avoids.
concepts.explanation: It is offered to make the document-level point concrete rather than as something BERT uses: its sentences are not in document order, so long contiguous spans cannot be recovered from it.

concepts.name: Generating a training input sequence
concepts.summary: Two spans are sampled, assigned the A and B embeddings, given the 50/50 NSP treatment, capped at 512 combined tokens, and then masked.
concepts.explanation: Each pre-training example is built in one pass so both objectives share it. The spans are called "sentences" although they are typically much longer, and LM masking is applied afterwards on WordPiece tokens at a uniform 15% rate. This is why one sequence supplies both masked-token predictions and one IsNext/NotNext decision.

concepts.name: 512-token maximum sequence length
concepts.summary: The two sampled spans are drawn so their combined length does not exceed 512 tokens.
concepts.explanation: 512 is the hard ceiling on what a pre-trained BERT can attend over, because that is the largest position for which a position embedding is learned. It also drives the length-schedule cost argument, since attention is quadratic in length, and it fixes the batch arithmetic: 256 sequences times 512 tokens is 128,000 tokens per batch.

concepts.name: 1,000,000 steps at 128,000 tokens per batch
concepts.summary: Pre-training runs for one million updates on 256-sequence batches, approximately 40 passes over the 3.3 billion word corpus.
concepts.explanation: The step count is the budget the paper controls; the epoch figure is derived from it and the corpus size. Forty passes is a lot of repetition, consistent with [[masked-language-model|MLM]] extracting signal from only 15% of positions per pass. Appendix C.1 examines what happens with fewer steps.

concepts.name: Adam settings for pre-training
concepts.summary: Adam with learning rate 1e-4, $\beta_1=0.9$, $\beta_2=0.999$, L2 weight decay 0.01, warmup over the first 10,000 steps then linear decay, and dropout 0.1 on all layers.
concepts.explanation: Warmup plus straight-line decay fixes the whole learning-rate trajectory from two numbers. The 1e-4 rate is two to five times larger than the fine-tuning rates. Dropout stays at 0.1 in every run, pre-training and fine-tuning alike; it is one of the few settings the paper does not vary.

concepts.name: gelu activation
concepts.summary: BERT uses the gelu activation rather than relu, following OpenAI GPT.
concepts.explanation: gelu is a smooth activation that scales an input by roughly the probability that a standard normal variable falls below it, so unlike relu it has no hard cutoff at zero and small negative inputs are attenuated rather than zeroed. The paper's stated reason for the choice is precedent, and no ablation of gelu against relu is reported.

citedFrom.refText: Dan Hendrycks and Kevin Gimpel. 2016. Bridging nonlinearities and stochastic regularizers with gaussian error linear units. CoRR, abs/1606.08415.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The activation used on every layer is named and adopted by precedent without the functional form or any motivation being given.

concepts.name: Combined MLM + NSP training loss
concepts.summary: The training loss is the sum of the mean masked LM likelihood and the mean next sentence prediction likelihood.
concepts.explanation: Both objectives are optimized at once on the same input sequence, with the two terms added and no weighting coefficient reported. The [[masked-language-model|MLM]] term averages over the roughly 15% of selected positions; the [[next-sentence-prediction|NSP]] term is a single binary prediction from $C$.

concepts.name: 128-then-512 sequence length schedule
concepts.summary: 90% of pre-training steps use length-128 sequences; the last 10% use length 512, specifically to learn the longer-range position embeddings.
concepts.explanation: The motivation is cost: attention is quadratic in length, so most training is done short. The final 10% at 512 exists because [[position-embeddings]] beyond 128 would otherwise never receive gradients. This is presented as a pragmatic speedup rather than a method contribution, and no comparison against training entirely at 512 is reported.

concepts.name: Fine-tuning BERT
concepts.summary: Adapting the pre-trained model to a task by plugging in task-specific inputs and outputs and training every parameter end-to-end.
concepts.explanation: The paper argues fine-tuning is straightforward because self-attention lets one model handle single texts and text pairs alike, so adapting means swapping the appropriate inputs and outputs. The A and B slots take sentence pairs, hypothesis-premise pairs, question-passage pairs, or a degenerate text-∅ pair; at the output, $C$ feeds a layer for sequence-level tasks and the $T_i$ for token-level ones. Nothing is frozen, which distinguishes this from feature-based use.

concepts.name: Plugging in task-specific inputs and outputs
concepts.summary: Task adaptation consists of mapping the task's texts onto the A/B slots and attaching an output layer to the right hidden vectors.
concepts.explanation: This is the mechanical content of fine-tuning. On the input side each task's texts are cast into the packed sequence format the model was pre-trained on; on the output side the only choice is which hidden vectors to read. Nothing inside the encoder changes, which is why so few parameters are learned from scratch.

concepts.name: Degenerate text-∅ pair
concepts.summary: Single-text tasks are handled by treating the input as a pair whose second half is empty.
concepts.explanation: Rather than defining a second input format for classification and tagging, the paper casts them as a text-∅ pair: the sequence holds only sentence A and the pair machinery goes unused. This keeps the [[input-representation]] uniform across all four task shapes.

concepts.name: Self-attention subsuming cross-attention
concepts.summary: The paper's argument that encoding a concatenated pair with self-attention already includes bidirectional cross attention between the two texts.
concepts.explanation: Because the pair is concatenated into one sequence and attention is unrestricted, every token of one text attends to every token of the other from the first layer, which the paper says effectively includes [[bidirectional-cross-attention]]. The payoff is that no pair-specific architecture has to be bolted on at fine-tuning time.

concepts.name: Bidirectional cross attention
concepts.summary: Attention computed between two separately encoded texts in both directions, the pattern BERT's concatenated encoding replaces.
concepts.explanation: In models like Parikh et al. (2016) and Seo et al. (2017), each text is encoded on its own and a dedicated attention layer then aligns the two. BERT has no such layer; the alignment happens inside ordinary self-attention over the joined sequence. The paper cites these as the pattern it departs from rather than describing them.

concepts.name: One additional output layer
concepts.summary: Task-specific models are formed by adding a single output layer to BERT, so a minimal number of parameters is learned from scratch.
concepts.explanation: For a sequence-level task this layer reads $C$ and produces class scores; for a token-level task it reads each $T_i$. Its parameters are the only ones initialised randomly at fine-tuning time; everything below is inherited and updated. This is the concrete form of the claim about minimal difference between pre-trained and downstream architectures.

concepts.name: End-to-end fine-tuning of all parameters
concepts.summary: Both the pre-trained encoder and the new output layer are trained together on the task's labeled data.
concepts.explanation: Nothing is frozen. This is the contrast with feature-based use, where the encoder's outputs are consumed as fixed features by a separate model, and it is the reason Section 5.2 hypothesises that fine-tuning scales better on small datasets.

concepts.name: Fine-tuning cost
concepts.summary: Every result in the paper can be reproduced in at most an hour on a single Cloud TPU, or a few hours on a GPU, starting from the pre-trained model.
concepts.explanation: The paper puts this next to a four-day pre-training run to make the point that the expensive step happens once. The SQuAD model is quoted at around 30 minutes on a single Cloud TPU to reach 91.0 Dev F1. The figure covers fine-tuning only and assumes the checkpoint already exists.

concepts.name: Fine-tuning hyperparameter grid
concepts.summary: Fine-tuning reuses the pre-training settings except batch size (16 or 32), Adam learning rate (5e-5, 3e-5 or 2e-5) and epochs (2, 3 or 4), searched over a small grid.
concepts.explanation: Appendix A.3 gives these as ranges that worked well across all tasks, with optimal values task-specific. The rates are all smaller than pre-training's 1e-4, which fits the situation: parameters start from a good point and the labeled data is limited. Two to four epochs is short, reflecting that most of the model's knowledge is already in the initialization.

concepts.name: Small datasets are more hyperparameter-sensitive
concepts.summary: The authors observed that large datasets, around 100k+ labeled examples, were far less sensitive to hyperparameter choice than small ones.
concepts.explanation: This is reported as an observation, not measured with numbers. Its consequence is that results on small downstream datasets depend more on the search than results on large ones, which is worth keeping in mind when reading the per-task tables.

concepts.name: Exhaustive search on the development set
concepts.summary: Because fine-tuning is cheap, every combination in the grid is run and the best model on dev is kept.
concepts.explanation: The grid is 2 batch sizes times 3 learning rates times 3 epoch counts, so 18 runs, each typically under an hour. Selection is by development set performance, keeping the test set clean. It is a reproducibility detail worth noting when comparing BERT's numbers to systems tuned less aggressively.

concepts.name: The eleven-task fine-tuning sweep
concepts.summary: BERT is evaluated by fine-tuning it on eleven NLP tasks, each with a small task-specific output layer on the same pre-trained encoder.
concepts.explanation: Section 4 covers the nine reported GLUE tasks, SQuAD v1.1 and v2.0, and SWAG, with [[conll-2003-ner|CoNLL-2003 NER]] appearing separately in the feature-based ablation. The point of the sweep is that one pre-trained model plus a handful of new parameters covers sentence classification, sentence-pair classification, span extraction and multiple choice. Each task differs only in how the input is packed and which output vectors are read. The count is the paper's evidence that one model can replace a family of specialised architectures.

concepts.name: GLUE benchmark
concepts.summary: A collection of sentence and sentence-pair understanding datasets under one submission format and leaderboard, used as BERT's main sentence-level testbed.
concepts.explanation: BERT fine-tunes on each GLUE task separately using the same [[input-representation]] and classification head, changing only the number of labels. The paper reports BERT_BASE and BERT_LARGE beating all prior systems on all reported tasks, with 4.5% and 7.0% average improvement over the previous state of the art. Section 2.2 notes GPT held the previous best on many of these, which is what makes it the natural comparison point.

concepts.name: GLUE leaderboard score
concepts.summary: The single aggregate number GLUE reports per system, averaging its per-task scores.
concepts.explanation: Because the tasks use different metrics and differ greatly in size, the aggregate is an average of per-task scores rather than a pooled accuracy, so a gain there can come from broad improvement or from large gains on a few tasks. The abstract reports 80.5%, a 7.7 point [[absolute-improvement]] over GPT's 72.8 as of the date of writing. The Table 1 numbers are taken from the public leaderboard and OpenAI's blog post rather than re-run.

concepts.name: GLUE evaluation server and hidden test labels
concepts.summary: GLUE does not distribute test labels; scores come from submitting predictions to a server, which limits how often a system can be evaluated on test.
concepts.explanation: All model selection therefore happens on the Dev sets. The paper states it made a single submission for each of BERT_BASE and BERT_LARGE, so the test numbers are not the best of many attempts, while every hyperparameter choice described was made on Dev.

concepts.name: C-vector classification head
concepts.summary: For GLUE, the final [CLS] vector is fed to one new linear layer with weights $W \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times H}$, trained with ordinary cross-entropy.
concepts.explanation: The input, single sentence or pair, is packed exactly as in Section 3, and $C$ is taken as the aggregate representation. The loss is written $\log(\mathrm{softmax}(CW^T))$ and the whole model including $W$ is trained jointly. Tasks differ only in $K$ — two for the binary tasks, three for MNLI, with STS-B a graded score. $W$ is the only new parameter matrix, and it is reinitialised on each random restart.

concepts.name: GLUE fine-tuning protocol
concepts.summary: Batch size 32 and 3 epochs for every task, with only the learning rate chosen per task from a small grid on Dev.
concepts.explanation: The rate is picked among 5e-5, 4e-5, 3e-5 and 2e-5. Holding everything else fixed across nine datasets is part of the paper's claim that BERT transfers without per-task engineering.

concepts.name: Random restarts for unstable fine-tuning
concepts.summary: BERT_LARGE fine-tuning was sometimes unstable on small datasets, so several restarts from the same checkpoint were run and the best kept on Dev.
concepts.explanation: A restart reuses the identical pre-trained weights and changes only the data shuffling and the classifier initialisation, so the spread comes entirely from the small random parts of the setup. The same device appears in Section 5.2, where each model-size cell is the average Dev accuracy over 5 restarts. The paper reports the instability as an observation and does not diagnose it.

concepts.name: MNLI (Multi-Genre NLI)
concepts.summary: A large crowdsourced entailment task over sentence pairs from multiple genres, with three labels.
concepts.explanation: MNLI is the largest and most widely reported GLUE task, which is why the abstract singles out its 86.7% accuracy and 4.6 point [[absolute-improvement]], and why MNLI Dev accuracy is the yardstick in the pre-training-task ablation, the model-size table, the training-steps curve and the masking ablation. Its multi-genre construction forces generalisation beyond one domain.

concepts.name: QQP (Quora Question Pairs)
concepts.summary: A binary task: decide whether two Quora questions are semantically equivalent.
concepts.explanation: Sentence-pair classification with two labels, using the same packed input and [CLS] head as the other pair tasks. It is one of the larger GLUE datasets and appears only as a column in Table 1.

concepts.name: QNLI (Question NLI)
concepts.summary: SQuAD recast as binary classification: does this sentence contain the answer to this question?
concepts.explanation: Negative pairs are drawn from the same paragraph as the positives, so the task is not solvable by topic matching alone. QNLI is one of the three tasks where the paper reports that removing [[next-sentence-prediction]] hurts significantly.

concepts.name: SST-2 (Stanford Sentiment Treebank)
concepts.summary: Binary single-sentence sentiment classification over sentences from movie reviews.
concepts.explanation: A single-sentence task, so the packed input has one segment and the [CLS] vector is the whole basis for the prediction. It appears in Table 1 and again as one of the four datasets in the model-size ablation. Section 2.1 also lists sentiment analysis among the benchmarks ELMo advanced.

concepts.name: CoLA (Corpus of Linguistic Acceptability)
concepts.summary: Binary single-sentence classification of whether an English sentence is linguistically acceptable.
concepts.explanation: The label is a grammaticality judgement rather than a meaning judgement, so it probes something closer to syntax. GLUE scores it with Matthews correlation rather than accuracy, which is what Table 1's column reports. It is small, and shows up in the model-size discussion as a task where BERT_LARGE still helps.

concepts.name: STS-B (Semantic Textual Similarity Benchmark)
concepts.summary: Sentence pairs from news headlines and other sources annotated with a 1-to-5 similarity score.
concepts.explanation: The target is graded rather than discrete, so it is the one GLUE task in the set that is naturally a regression, scored by correlation with the human ratings. It is small, and one of the tasks the paper points to when arguing BERT_LARGE helps where training data is scarce.

concepts.name: MRPC (Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus)
concepts.summary: Sentence pairs automatically extracted from online news, human-annotated for whether the two mean the same thing.
concepts.explanation: MRPC has 3,600 labelled training examples, and the paper singles it out twice: as a task where the left-to-right ablation model drops sharply, and as the case where increasing model size still improves accuracy despite tiny training data and a task quite different from the pre-training objectives. Its size is what makes it a useful stress test.

concepts.name: RTE (Recognizing Textual Entailment)
concepts.summary: A binary entailment task similar to MNLI but with much less training data.
concepts.explanation: Because it is small and shares its label semantics with MNLI, it is the clearest case where extra supervision from a related task helps: the paper notes substantial improvements on RTE from multi-task training with MNLI, while reporting only single-task numbers. That is a footnote aside, so the size of the improvement is not quantified.

concepts.name: WNLI (Winograd NLI) and why it is excluded
concepts.summary: A small inference set built from Winograd schemas, dropped from the reported results because its construction is known to be problematic.
concepts.explanation: The GLUE webpage notes issues with how it was built, and the paper states that every trained system submitted to GLUE has scored worse than the 65.1 accuracy of always predicting the majority class. The authors exclude it, saying this is to be fair to [[openai-gpt]], and for their own submission they always predicted the majority class. This is why the sweep is described as eleven tasks while GLUE nominally has nine.

concepts.name: Majority-class baseline
concepts.summary: Always predicting the most frequent label, used as the floor a real system must beat.
concepts.explanation: When a benchmark's trained systems sit below this baseline, as the paper reports for WNLI, the benchmark is measuring something other than model quality.

concepts.name: Single-task fine-tuning (and the multi-task aside)
concepts.summary: All reported GLUE numbers come from fine-tuning one model per task; multi-task fine-tuning is mentioned only as an untested possibility.
concepts.explanation: Each Table 1 result is a separate run from the same pre-trained checkpoint. The paper notes a multi-task approach could push performance further and reports observing gains on RTE from training with MNLI, but includes no such results. Keeping the reported setup single-task means the comparison against prior systems is not confounded by extra labelled data.

concepts.name: SQuAD v1.1
concepts.summary: Over 100,000 crowdsourced question/answer pairs where the answer is a span of a given Wikipedia passage.
concepts.explanation: Every question in v1.1 is answerable, so a system only has to locate the span, not decide whether one exists. Because the output is a pair of positions rather than a class label, SQuAD is where the paper introduces a token-level output head instead of a [CLS] head. It reports beating the top leaderboard entry by +1.5 F1 as an ensemble and +1.3 F1 as a single system, with the single model exceeding the top prior ensemble on F1; the abstract quotes 93.2 Test F1.

concepts.name: Answer span
concepts.summary: A contiguous stretch of passage tokens, identified by start and end positions, that constitutes the answer.
concepts.explanation: Predicting a span rather than generating text means the model never produces words, only picks two indices, which reduces QA to two classification problems over passage positions. The formulation is what makes BERT's per-token final hidden vectors, rather than the aggregate [CLS] vector, the right thing to read.

concepts.name: Question and passage as one packed sequence
concepts.summary: Question and passage are concatenated into a single input, the question tagged with the A segment embedding and the passage with B.
concepts.explanation: BERT does not encode them separately and then compare; both go through the same encoder in one sequence, so self-attention can relate any question token to any passage token at every layer. This is the sentence-pair mechanism reused unchanged for QA.

concepts.name: Start/end vector span prediction head
concepts.summary: SQuAD fine-tuning adds only two vectors, $S$ and $E$, whose dot products with each token's final hidden vector give start and end distributions over the passage.
concepts.explanation: No matrix and no extra layer: $P_i = e^{S \cdot T_i} / \sum_j e^{S \cdot T_j}$ for starts and the same form with $E$ for ends. Training sums the log-likelihoods of the correct start and correct end, treating them as two independent softmax problems with no term rewarding the pair jointly. Fine-tuning runs 3 epochs at learning rate 5e-5 with batch size 32. This is the extraction counterpart of the [CLS] head, and SQuAD 2.0 extends it rather than replacing it.

concepts.name: Start vector S and end vector E
concepts.summary: The only task-specific parameters introduced for SQuAD: two $H$-dimensional vectors, one scoring each token as a span start, one as an end.
concepts.explanation: Each is a single learned direction in the model's hidden space, so scoring a token is one dot product. Together they are on the order of $2H$ new parameters, negligible against 110M or 340M, and they are trained jointly with the whole encoder rather than on top of a frozen model.

concepts.name: Span score and maximum-scoring-span decoding
concepts.summary: A candidate span from $i$ to $j$ scores $S \cdot T_i + E \cdot T_j$, and the prediction is the highest-scoring span with $j \geq i$.
concepts.explanation: Because start and end are scored independently and added, the best span is found by searching position pairs rather than by any sequence decoding. The only constraint stated is $j \geq i$, applied at decoding time and not during training. The score used for decoding is the sum of raw dot products, not of softmax probabilities.

concepts.name: TriviaQA data augmentation
concepts.summary: Before fine-tuning on SQuAD, the model is first fine-tuned on TriviaQA, described as modest data augmentation to match leaderboard systems that may use any public data.
concepts.explanation: The data used is paragraphs from TriviaQA-Wiki formed from the first 400 tokens of documents containing at least one provided possible answer. The paper reports that removing this stage costs only 0.1 to 0.4 F1, so the augmentation is not what carries the result, and it is not used for the SQuAD 2.0 model.

citedFrom.refText: Mandar Joshi, Eunsol Choi, Daniel S Weld, and Luke Zettlemoyer. 2017. TriviaQA: A large scale distantly supervised challenge dataset for reading comprehension. In ACL.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The augmentation is specified only as filtered TriviaQA-Wiki paragraphs; reproducing it or judging what supervision it adds needs the dataset's distant-supervision construction.

concepts.name: Exact Match and F1 on SQuAD
concepts.summary: SQuAD's two metrics: EM counts a prediction correct only on an exact match, F1 gives partial credit for token overlap.
concepts.explanation: F1 is computed over the tokens shared between the predicted span and the reference, so overlapping predictions still score. All of the paper's SQuAD comparisons are quoted in F1, and the τ threshold in SQuAD 2.0 is tuned on Dev specifically to maximise it.

concepts.name: SQuAD leaderboard conditions
concepts.summary: Top leaderboard entries have no up-to-date public system descriptions and may train on any public data, which shapes how the comparison is set up.
concepts.explanation: The paper flags both facts as reasons its comparison is imperfect, and gives them as the motivation for the TriviaQA stage. It also notes that QANet is described in a published paper but that the system has improved substantially since publication, so leaderboard entry and paper are not the same system.

concepts.name: Prior published SQuAD systems
concepts.summary: The published baselines Table 2 compares against, mostly purpose-built reading comprehension architectures with attention machinery between question and passage.
concepts.explanation: Table 2 lists BiDAF (Seo et al., 2017), the multi-paragraph reader of Clark and Gardner (2018), an ELMo-based system, and Reinforced Mnemonic Reader; QANet is named in a footnote. The contrast being drawn is between these task-specific architectures and BERT's two extra vectors on a general pre-trained encoder.

concepts.name: SQuAD v2.0
concepts.summary: SQuAD extended so a question may have no short answer in the paragraph, which the paper calls more realistic.
concepts.explanation: A system must now decide whether an answer exists, so a confident-looking span is no longer automatically the right output. The paper extends its v1.1 model rather than building a new one, and reports a +5.1 F1 improvement over the previous best while excluding systems that already use BERT as a component; the abstract quotes 83.1 Test F1. Fine-tuning ran 2 epochs at 5e-5 with batch size 48, with no TriviaQA data.

concepts.name: Unanswerable questions
concepts.summary: Questions for which the paragraph contains no short answer; the correct output is an abstention.
concepts.explanation: A model trained only on answerable questions has no way to express "no answer", so an output slot for abstention has to be added and a decision rule has to say when to use it. The paper's answer to both is the [CLS]-as-null-span trick plus a tuned threshold.

concepts.name: [CLS] as the null span
concepts.summary: Unanswerable questions are treated as having a span that starts and ends at [CLS], so abstention becomes another position in the same probability space.
concepts.explanation: The start and end distributions are extended to include the [CLS] position, which is always present and never part of the passage. Training then needs no new loss term: an unanswerable example simply has gold start and end at index 0. This reuses the v1.1 head unchanged, which is why the paper calls it simple, and at prediction time the null option competes with real spans through a score comparison rather than a separate classifier.

concepts.name: Null score s_null
concepts.summary: The score of abstaining, $s_{null} = S \cdot C + E \cdot C$, computed with the same start and end vectors against the [CLS] representation.
concepts.explanation: Because it is built from the same $S$ and $E$ as every other span score, it is directly comparable on the same scale. The best non-null span score is $\hat{s}_{i,j} = \max_{j \geq i} S \cdot T_i + E \cdot T_j$.

concepts.name: Threshold τ for answering
concepts.summary: A non-null answer is predicted only when $\hat{s}_{i,j} > s_{null} + \tau$, with τ chosen on dev to maximise F1.
concepts.explanation: Without τ the comparison would be a plain argmax between null and best span; τ shifts the operating point toward answering or abstaining, which matters because the metric weights the two error types in a particular way. Tuning it on Dev to maximise F1 means it is fitted to the metric rather than derived from the model, and the paper reports it as such.

concepts.name: SWAG (Situations With Adversarial Generations)
concepts.summary: 113k sentence-pair completion examples: given a sentence, choose the most plausible of four continuations.
concepts.explanation: The candidates are constructed adversarially, so surface cues are meant to be unreliable. The paper reports BERT_LARGE beating the dataset authors' ESIM+ELMo baseline by 27.1% and [[openai-gpt]] by 8.3%; ESIM+ELMo is a feature-based system, so part of the gap is attributable to more than one difference at once. Fine-tuning used 3 epochs, learning rate 2e-5, batch size 16.

concepts.name: Grounded commonsense inference
concepts.summary: Judging which continuation of a described situation is plausible, using everyday knowledge rather than logical entailment.
concepts.explanation: The distinction from [[natural-language-inference]] is that no candidate is strictly entailed or contradicted; the model is ranking plausibility. The signal therefore has to come from what pre-training taught the model about how situations unfold. This is the framing SWAG's authors give the task, and the paper adopts it.

concepts.name: Four packed sequences scored by one vector
concepts.summary: Each candidate continuation is packed with the context into its own sequence; one learned vector dotted with each sequence's [CLS] representation gives four scores, normalised by softmax.
concepts.explanation: The context becomes sentence A and a candidate becomes sentence B, so the model encodes four separate sequences and never sees the alternatives side by side. The only task-specific parameters are that one vector, and the comparison between choices happens at the very top, in the softmax, not inside the encoder.

concepts.name: BERT's ablation programme
concepts.summary: Experiments that remove or vary one facet of BERT at a time to see how much each contributes.
concepts.explanation: Section 5 covers three: the pre-training objectives, model size, and fine-tuning versus feature-based use. Appendix C adds two more: how many pre-training steps are needed, and how the masking mixture is chosen. Each holds the pre-training data, fine-tuning scheme and hyperparameters fixed so the changed facet is the only difference. Several run on Dev sets and on a subset of tasks, so they are evidence about relative importance rather than headline results.

concepts.name: Effect of pre-training tasks
