concepts.summary: Two cut-down objectives, No NSP and LTR & No NSP, trained under identical conditions to isolate what next sentence prediction and bidirectionality each buy.
concepts.explanation: Both variants use exactly the same data, fine-tuning scheme and hyperparameters as BERT_BASE, so the only difference is the objective. Comparing BERT_BASE with [[no-nsp-ablation|No NSP]] isolates [[next-sentence-prediction|NSP]]; comparing No NSP with LTR & No NSP isolates bidirectionality. The paper reports that removing NSP hurts significantly on QNLI, MNLI and SQuAD 1.1, and that the LTR model is worse on all tasks, with large drops on [[mrpc]] and SQuAD. Appendix A.4 leans on this ablation to argue the four uncontrolled BERT/GPT differences are secondary.

concepts.name: No NSP
concepts.summary: A bidirectional model pre-trained with the masked LM objective but without next sentence prediction.
concepts.explanation: It keeps everything else, so it still sees packed two-segment inputs and still learns from masked tokens. The tasks it loses most on — QNLI, MNLI, SQuAD 1.1 — all take pairs as input, which is consistent with [[next-sentence-prediction|NSP]] being what teaches the model to relate two segments. It also serves as the bidirectional control for the left-to-right comparison, so that comparison is not contaminated by NSP.

concepts.name: LTR & No NSP
concepts.summary: A left-context-only model trained with a standard left-to-right language model and no NSP; the closest in-house stand-in for OpenAI GPT.
concepts.explanation: The left-only constraint is kept at fine-tuning as well as pre-training, because removing it introduced a mismatch that degraded results. The paper describes the variant as directly comparable to GPT but using BERT's larger dataset, [[input-representation]] and fine-tuning scheme, which makes it cleaner than the published GPT numbers. It is worse on all tasks; for SQuAD the paper says the failure is intuitively clear, since token-level states have no right-side context when scoring a span boundary.

concepts.name: BiLSTM on top of the LTR model
concepts.summary: A randomly initialised BiLSTM added above the left-to-right model as a good-faith attempt to supply right-side context; it partly repairs SQuAD but not GLUE.
concepts.explanation: The paper reports that it does significantly improve SQuAD results but they remain far worse than the pre-trained bidirectional models, and that it hurts on the GLUE tasks. The reading offered is that bidirectionality added on top, after pre-training and with random weights, is not a substitute for bidirectionality present at every layer during pre-training.

concepts.name: Effect of model size
concepts.summary: Models of varying L, H and A are compared; larger is strictly better on all four GLUE tasks tested, including very small ones.
concepts.explanation: All variants share hyperparameters and training procedure, and each cell is the average Dev accuracy over 5 random restarts. The paper says it believes this is the first work to demonstrate convincingly that scaling to extreme model sizes also leads to large improvements on very small scale tasks, provided the model has been sufficiently pre-trained — presented as a belief about the literature, not a proof, on evidence of four datasets including [[mrpc]] with 3,600 examples. Held-out LM perplexity is reported alongside to show the familiar large-scale effect is present too, so the new claim is specifically about small downstream tasks.

concepts.name: Prior mixed evidence on scaling
concepts.summary: Two earlier feature-based results that found limited or no downstream benefit from bigger pre-trained models.
concepts.explanation: Peters et al. (2018b) presented mixed results from increasing bi-LM size from two to four layers, and Melamud et al. (2016) mentioned in passing that raising [[hidden-size-h|hidden size]] from 200 to 600 helped but 1,000 did not. The paper notes both used a [[feature-based-approach|feature-based approach]] and uses that as the wedge for its own hypothesis about why fine-tuning behaves differently.

concepts.name: Why fine-tuning may scale better on small data
concepts.summary: The paper hypothesises that because fine-tuning adds very few randomly initialised parameters, task models can exploit large pre-trained representations even when task data is tiny.
concepts.explanation: The contrast is with feature-based setups, where a whole task architecture with many fresh parameters has to be fit on the small dataset and a bigger frozen representation just widens its input. When nearly all parameters start from pre-training, extra capacity arrives already trained. The paper labels this a hypothesis and does not test it separately.

concepts.name: Feature-based approach with BERT
concepts.summary: Using BERT as a frozen feature extractor rather than fine-tuning it, tested on CoNLL-2003 NER to see how much is lost.
concepts.explanation: Two motivations are given: not all tasks can be easily represented by a [[transformer-encoder]], so some need a task-specific model on top; and there are computational benefits to pre-computing an expensive representation once and running many cheap experiments on it. Activations are extracted from one or more layers with no BERT parameters fine-tuned. The best configuration lands 0.3 F1 behind fine-tuning the whole model, which the paper reads as BERT being effective in both modes.

concepts.name: Two-layer 768-dimensional BiLSTM over frozen features
concepts.summary: In the feature-based setting the extracted embeddings feed a randomly initialised two-layer 768-dimensional BiLSTM before the classification layer.
concepts.explanation: Because BERT's parameters are frozen, all task learning happens in this stack, so it needs enough capacity to be a fair test, and none of it benefits from pre-training. It is the [[task-specific-architecture|task-specific architecture]] the paper said some tasks require, made concrete.

concepts.name: Which layers to extract features from
concepts.summary: Feature-based results are compared across choices of which hidden layers to tap, from the last layer alone to concatenations of several.
concepts.explanation: Since BERT's layers are not alike, where to tap the network is itself a hyperparameter in this setting, and Table 7 reports several variants. The paper states the best method concatenates the token representations from the top four hidden layers, ending only 0.3 F1 behind full fine-tuning. It does not offer an account of why four.

concepts.name: Concatenating the top four hidden layers
concepts.summary: The best-performing feature extraction: join each token's vectors from the top four layers into one longer vector.
concepts.explanation: Concatenating rather than summing keeps each layer's information separately available to the classifier above, at the cost of a four-times-wider input. It is adopted as the default wherever the paper uses BERT feature-based elsewhere, including the masking ablation's feature-based column.

concepts.name: Effect of number of pre-training steps
concepts.summary: MNLI Dev accuracy after fine-tuning from checkpoints pre-trained for k steps, asking whether BERT's full budget is needed.
concepts.explanation: Figure 5 plots the curve, and the paper's answer is yes: BERT_BASE gains almost 1.0% additional MNLI accuracy at 1M steps compared to 500k. That is substantial extra compute for one accuracy point, and the paper reports the trade-off without arguing it is optimal. The same figure answers the second question, about [[masked-language-model|MLM]] convergence speed.

concepts.name: Ablation for different masking procedures
concepts.summary: Varying the probabilities of the three masking strategies, to check whether the 80/10/10 mixture matters.
concepts.explanation: Table 8 reports Dev results on MNLI and on NER, with both fine-tuning and feature-based numbers for NER. The summary is that fine-tuning is surprisingly robust to different masking strategies, that using only the MASK strategy was problematic for feature-based NER as expected, and that using only RND performs much worse than the chosen mixture — the last described as interesting rather than explained.

concepts.name: MASK, SAME and RND
concepts.summary: The three things that can happen to a token selected for prediction: replace with [MASK], keep as is, or replace with a random token.
concepts.explanation: These are Table 8's column labels, with BERT at 80/10/10. SAME and RND both mean the model sees a real-looking token at a position it must still predict, which is what forces it to keep a useful representation of every token rather than only of masked slots. Each row of the table is a different probability assignment.

concepts.name: Why the feature-based setting amplifies the mismatch
concepts.summary: With BERT frozen, the model cannot adapt to the absence of [MASK] at test time, so a masking mismatch shows up more sharply.
concepts.explanation: When fine-tuning, the encoder's weights move during task training and can absorb the distribution shift between pre-training inputs and real inputs. Frozen, whatever the objective baked in is what the classifier gets. The paper predicts this in advance and reports it borne out: MASK-only is problematic for feature-based NER while fine-tuning stays robust.

concepts.name: Development set and dev-set model selection
concepts.summary: The held-out split used for choosing hyperparameters and variants, separate from the test set that reports final numbers.
concepts.explanation: The paper selects on dev for the GLUE learning rate, for choosing among random restarts, for the SQuAD 2.0 threshold, for the per-task fine-tuning rate noted in A.4, and for every ablation number in Section 5 and Appendix C. It matters here because GLUE withholds test labels entirely, so dev is the only surface available for tuning.

concepts.name: F1 score
concepts.summary: The harmonic mean of precision and recall, used here as the span-overlap metric for SQuAD and the evaluation metric for NER.
concepts.explanation: For SQuAD, precision and recall are computed over the tokens shared between the predicted span and the reference, so partial overlaps get partial credit.

concepts.name: State of the art
concepts.summary: The best published result on a benchmark at the time of writing.
concepts.explanation: Claims of state of the art are relative to a leaderboard snapshot and to whatever comparison conditions the leaderboard enforces.

concepts.name: Absolute improvement
concepts.summary: A gain stated as the arithmetic difference between two scores, in points, rather than as a percentage of the previous score.
concepts.explanation: The abstract's "7.7% point absolute improvement" means the [[glue-score]] went from 72.8 to 80.5, not that it rose by 7.7% of its old value. The distinction matters at high scores, where a small absolute gain can be a large relative reduction in remaining error.

concepts.name: LSTM
concepts.summary: A recurrent cell with gating, the standard sequence encoder in the work that preceded the Transformer.
concepts.explanation: Mentioned in Section 2.1 as what context2vec uses to read left and right context. Assumed background here.

concepts.name: BiLSTM
concepts.summary: A recurrent layer run in both directions over a sequence, with the two directions' outputs joined per position.
concepts.explanation: It appears twice in the experiments as the thing added on top of a model that cannot see both directions on its own: over the LTR ablation model in Section 5.1, and over frozen BERT features in Section 5.3. In both cases it is randomly initialised, so it carries no pre-trained knowledge.

concepts.name: Cloud TPU
concepts.summary: The accelerator hardware the paper's training costs are quoted against; a Cloud TPU here is four chips.
concepts.explanation: Pre-training used 4 Cloud TPUs (16 chips) for BERT_BASE and 16 (64 chips) for BERT_LARGE, four days each. Fine-tuning is quoted at at most one hour on a single Cloud TPU. The units matter mainly for reading the cost claims.

concepts.name: Ensembling
concepts.summary: Combining several trained models' predictions into one, usually scoring better than any single model.
concepts.explanation: The SQuAD leaderboard separates single-model and ensemble entries. The paper's point in Section 4.2 is comparative: its single model outperforms the top prior ensemble on F1, and its own ensemble goes further.
